stem: Explain antibiotic resistance observed in bacteria in light of Darwinian selection theory.
solution:
Antibiotic resistance is **natural selection** acting on **heritable variation** in a bacterial population: the antibiotic does not create resistance, it **selects** the resistant variants that already exist.

1. **Variation:** a bacterial population has built-in variation. By **chance mutation**, a few cells may already be able to survive a given antibiotic.
2. **Changed environment:** when the antibiotic is applied, the conditions change. The sensitive bacteria are killed, and only that part of the population which can survive the new conditions (the resistant variants) is left.
3. **Selection for fitness:** the resistant bacteria are better fit under the new conditions, so they survive and leave more progeny. Fitness, in Darwinian terms, is **reproductive fitness**.
4. **Inheritance:** resistance is **inherited** (it has a genetic basis), so it passes to the progeny of the survivors.
5. **Rapid change:** bacteria divide fast and multiply into millions of individuals within hours, so the resistant variant soon outgrows the others and the population becomes resistant.

Thus excess use of antibiotics selects resistant varieties in a time scale of **months or years, not centuries**. It is an example of **evolution by anthropogenic action**, and shows that evolution is not directed but a **stochastic process** based on chance mutation and selection.
groundedIn: §6.3; §6.5; §6.2; §6.7 — resistant microbes against antibiotics appear in months or years, evolution by anthropogenic action, stochastic process based on chance mutation (§6.3); bacterial colony with built-in variation, a change in the medium brings out the part that can survive, fitness is inherited with a genetic basis, microbes multiply into millions within hours (§6.5); fitness is reproductive fitness, natural selection (§6.2); pre-existing advantageous mutations when selected give new phenotypes (§6.7)

stem: Attempt giving a clear definition of the term species.
solution:
A **species** is a group of natural populations whose members resemble one another closely and **interbreed** among themselves to produce **fertile offspring**, and which is **reproductively isolated** from other such groups. This is the **biological species concept** (Ernst Mayr).

Members of a species share a common **gene pool**. A new species arises when the allele frequencies of a population change so much (for example through genetic drift and the founder effect) that it becomes a different species.
groundedIn: §6.7; §6.5 — gene pool; when the change in allele frequency is so different in the new population, they become a different species (founder effect) (§6.7); a variant population outgrows the others and appears as new species (§6.5); BEYOND CHAPTER: species as a group of interbreeding natural populations producing fertile offspring and reproductively isolated from other groups (biological species concept, Ernst Mayr)

stem: Try to trace the various components of human evolution (hint: brain size and function, skeletal structure, dietary preference, etc.)
solution:
Human evolution can be traced through a series of stages, each showing changes in brain size, posture and diet.

| Stage | Time | Brain size | Skeleton and posture | Diet and way of life |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus | About 15 mya | - | Hairy; walked like gorillas and chimpanzees. Ramapithecus more man-like, Dryopithecus more ape-like | - |
| Man-like primates (fossils from Ethiopia and Tanzania) | About 3-4 mya | - | Not taller than 4 feet, but walked upright | Lived in eastern Africa |
| Australopithecines | About 2 mya | - | - | Hunted with stone weapons but essentially ate fruit; East African grasslands |
| Homo habilis (first human-like being, the hominid) | - | 650-800 cc | - | Probably did not eat meat |
| Homo erectus (fossils found in Java, 1891) | About 1.5 mya | Around 900 cc | - | Probably ate meat |
| Neanderthal man | 1,00,000-40,000 years back (near east and central Asia) | 1400 cc | - | Used hides to protect the body; buried their dead |
| Homo sapiens | Modern Homo sapiens arose during the ice age, 75,000-10,000 years ago | - | - | Arose in Africa, spread across continents; cave art about 18,000 years ago; agriculture and settlements about 10,000 years back |

**Trends:**
1. **Brain size and function:** brain capacity increased (650-800 cc in Homo habilis, about 900 cc in Homo erectus, 1400 cc in Neanderthal man). The evolution of modern man parallels the evolution of the human brain and **language**, ending in a species with language skills and self-consciousness.
2. **Skeletal structure:** from hairy primates that walked like gorillas and chimpanzees to man-like primates that **walked upright**. The skull of a baby chimpanzee is more like the adult human skull than the adult chimpanzee skull (Fig. 6.11).
3. **Dietary preference:** from essentially fruit-eating forms (Australopithecines, Homo habilis, which probably did not eat meat) to **meat-eating** Homo erectus.
4. **Culture:** stone weapons, use of hides, burial of the dead, cave art (for example at Bhimbetka rock shelter, Madhya Pradesh) and finally agriculture and settled life.
groundedIn: §6.9; Fig. 6.11; §6.8 — Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus about 15 mya; man-like primates 3-4 mya walked upright, not taller than 4 feet; Australopithecines 2 mya, stone weapons but ate fruit; Homo habilis 650-800cc, did not eat meat; Homo erectus 1.5 mya, 900cc, ate meat; Neanderthal 1400cc, hides, buried dead; modern Homo sapiens 75,000-10,000 years ago, cave art 18,000 years ago, Bhimbetka, agriculture 10,000 years back (§6.9); baby chimpanzee skull more like adult human skull (Fig. 6.11); evolution of man with language skills and self-consciousness (§6.8); evolution of modern man parallels evolution of human brain and language (stated in the chapter Summary)

stem: Describe one example of adaptive radiation.
solution:
**Adaptive radiation** is the process of evolution of different species in a given geographical area starting from a point and literally radiating to other areas of geography (habitats).

**Example: Darwin's finches of the Galapagos Islands**

1. During his journey, Darwin visited the **Galapagos Islands** and found many varieties of small black birds, later called **Darwin's finches**, on the same island.
2. He conjectured that all these varieties evolved **on the island itself** from a common ancestral stock.
3. The original finches had **seed-eating** features (beaks suited to seeds).
4. From them, many other forms with **altered beaks** arose, which enabled them to become **insectivorous** and **vegetarian** finches (Fig. 6.5).
5. Each form became adapted to a different food and habitat, so from one starting point the finches radiated into many species within one geographical area.

Darwin's finches are one of the best examples of adaptive radiation. (Another example is the Australian marsupials, which evolved from an ancestral stock into many different forms within the Australian island continent.)
groundedIn: §6.4; Fig. 6.5; Fig. 6.6 — Darwin at Galapagos Islands; small black birds called Darwin's finches; many varieties evolved on the island itself; original seed-eating features, altered beaks gave insectivorous and vegetarian finches; definition of adaptive radiation; Australian marsupials evolved from an ancestral stock

stem: Can we call human evolution as adaptive radiation?
solution:
**No.** Human evolution cannot be called adaptive radiation.

1. **Adaptive radiation** is the evolution of **many different species** from one ancestral stock in a given **geographical area**, starting from a point and radiating into different habitats, as in Darwin's finches of the Galapagos or the marsupials of Australia.
2. **Human evolution** is a **sequence of stages** over time along one line: Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus, man-like primates of eastern Africa, Australopithecines, Homo habilis, Homo erectus, Neanderthal man and finally Homo sapiens.
3. It did not produce a group of different species, each adapted to a different habitat in one area. Today only **one species, Homo sapiens**, survives.
4. Homo sapiens arose in Africa and moved across continents, developing into distinct **races**, not into separate species.

Hence human evolution is a progressive, step-wise evolution of a single lineage, not a radiation of many species from a common ancestor in one geographical area.
groundedIn: §6.4; §6.9 — adaptive radiation is the evolution of different species in a given geographical area starting from a point and radiating to other habitats; Darwin's finches and Australian marsupials (§6.4); stages Dryopithecus/Ramapithecus, man-like primates, Australopithecines, Homo habilis, Homo erectus, Neanderthal, Homo sapiens; Homo sapiens arose in Africa, moved across continents and developed into distinct races (§6.9)
